quiz.question: Codex confidently summarizes a project you cannot find in the open folder. What is the next useful action?
options: Ask it to build the full app anyway.
Confirm the working directory and inspect the named files.
Change to the most expensive model.
quiz.explanation: The mismatch is an environment problem until the folder and evidence are confirmed. A different model does not establish access.

quiz.question: Which statement about /diff is accurate?
options: It automatically proves the code is correct.
It restores every modified file.
It helps inspect changes; tests and acceptance remain separate.
quiz.explanation: A diff shows what changed. It does not prove runtime behavior or undo the working tree.

quiz.question: What is the recommended starting point for a new reusable Codex workflow?
options: A focused skill with a clear description and SKILL.md.
A new Claude slash-command namespace.
A global script with permission to publish by default.
quiz.explanation: Current Codex documentation recommends skills; their scope should remain proportional to the actual workflow.

quiz.question: A server is listed, but the ticket lookup returns an authorization error. What should the answer claim?
options: The ticket is probably closed.
The connection exists, but this record was not retrieved.
The ticket was verified because the server name appeared.
quiz.explanation: Listing a server does not prove access to a record. The failed lookup must remain a reported gap.

quiz.question: Which test best demonstrates that readme-check works?
options: Its folder has a professional-looking name.
The YAML parses without an error.
It detects a planted setup mismatch and does not edit the repository.
quiz.explanation: A behavioral test checks both useful findings and the workflow boundary; file validity alone is not enough.

quiz.question: A lint check passes after a filter fix. What remains necessary?
options: Check the original failing filter example and inspect the delivered change.
Nothing; lint proves the customer’s expected behavior.
Publish immediately before the preview is inspected.
quiz.explanation: Lint is useful but does not necessarily exercise the reported failure or establish acceptance of the result.

quiz.question: Where should a team’s mandatory test command primarily live?
options: Only in the agent’s generated memories.
In reviewed project guidance or checked-in documentation.
Only in a chat that one person remembers.
quiz.explanation: Mandatory guidance needs an explicit, reviewable source. Memory is an optional recall layer, not the only home for a rule.

quiz.question: The generated AGENTS.md says npm test, but package.json has no test script. What should you do?
options: Keep it because initialization is always authoritative.
Install a testing framework immediately.
Correct or remove the unsupported instruction and record the actual project state.
quiz.explanation: Initialization is a draft. Instructions must reflect the repository rather than inventing its tooling.

quiz.question: A directory contains both AGENTS.md and a nonempty AGENTS.override.md. Which is selected there?
options: Both are concatenated in that same directory.
AGENTS.override.md is selected for that directory.
Every parent instruction is automatically discarded.
quiz.explanation: Codex selects at most one file per directory, preferring the override; applicable parent files remain part of the chain.

quiz.question: Where should “use descriptive section headings” go?
options: In AGENTS.md or a referenced writing guide.
In a prefix_rule that allows all PowerShell commands.
In an API token value.
quiz.explanation: A writing convention is prose guidance. Execution policy and credentials serve different purposes.

quiz.question: Which claim is justified after a memory-enabled chat ends?
options: Its content has definitely been saved immediately.
It may become an input for later background memory generation.
Its decisions now override the current repository instructions.
quiz.explanation: Generation is asynchronous and eligibility-dependent; current source evidence and required guidance still matter.

quiz.question: Forking a chat is sufficient to undo which of these automatically?
options: Every file written after the fork point.
A message already sent to an external service.
Neither; conversation branching alone establishes no file or external rollback.
quiz.explanation: A fork copies conversation history. File and external-state recovery require their own verified mechanisms.

quiz.question: Why can git status show a file that ordinary git diff does not display?
options: The file may be untracked.
Git status always invents extra files.
The file is guaranteed to have no useful content.
quiz.explanation: Untracked files are reported by status but are not included in a normal working-tree diff until separately handled.

quiz.question: You want to reject one heading change while retaining a useful new paragraph. What is best?
options: Reset every repository file to the previous commit.
Inspect the diff and apply a targeted heading correction.
Start a new chat and assume the files revert.
quiz.explanation: A targeted correction preserves the useful work; a whole-file restore or broad reset can discard more than intended.

quiz.question: When does a chat fork guarantee independent file edits?
options: Whenever the conversation has a new name.
Only when the work is actually separated into an appropriate checkout or workflow.
Whenever the agent says the approaches are different.
quiz.explanation: Separate transcript IDs do not isolate a shared directory. Verify the actual filesystem boundary.

quiz.question: A baseline commit exists. Which statement is safest?
options: Every local file and external action can be restored from it.
The committed files have a recorded version; other state must be checked separately.
The task is automatically deployed and accepted.
quiz.explanation: A commit protects the file content it contains, not every local artifact or external system.

quiz.question: Which entry point is intended for a bounded non-interactive Codex task?
options: codex exec
claude -p
/new typed directly into PowerShell
quiz.explanation: codex exec is the documented scripted entry point; the other examples belong to another product or to the interactive composer.

quiz.question: What does a successful codex login status check establish?
options: Every MCP server can retrieve every record.
Local credentials are present; other access still depends on the task and environment.
The current repository has passed its tests.
quiz.explanation: Authentication status is one layer. Tool authorization, project access and task verification remain separate.

quiz.question: Why is --cd useful in a learning exercise?
options: It grants permission to publish externally.
It disables all repository instructions.
It makes the intended working directory explicit for that invocation.
quiz.explanation: An explicit directory reduces environment ambiguity; it does not grant unrelated authority or replace instruction discovery.

quiz.question: What does --output-schema primarily constrain?
options: The final response structure.
Whether every returned claim is true.
Whether the application has been deployed.
quiz.explanation: A schema constrains fields and types. Facts still need reconciliation with the source and the task still needs verification.

quiz.question: Which is the best first scripted task?
options: Improve everything and publish the result.
Summarize one selected local diff into a draft that you inspect.
Rotate credentials whenever a command fails.
quiz.explanation: A selected local diff gives a bounded source and an inspectable drafting output, making usefulness and correctness easier to assess.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest reason to create a skill?
options: One response needs a shorter opening.
A recurring task has stable inputs, an output format and checks.
A service is inaccessible and needs credentials.
quiz.explanation: A skill can reuse a proven procedure. It does not solve authentication or justify packaging every one-off edit.

quiz.question: The skill is selected correctly but invents missing README commands. What should you investigate first?
options: The color of its icon.
A larger global description budget.
Its evidence rules and execution instructions.
quiz.explanation: Selection worked. The observed failure is in how the procedure gathers evidence and handles missing information.

quiz.question: What proves more than successful skill discovery?
options: A report whose claims match the supplied files and whose side effects match the task.
A correctly spelled SKILL.md filename alone.
A confident summary that the skill is production-ready.
quiz.explanation: A discovered package can still execute the wrong procedure. Check evidence and actual behavior.

quiz.question: What does allow_implicit_invocation: false establish?
options: The skill cannot make file changes under any circumstances.
The skill is hidden from every user and client.
Codex will not choose the skill implicitly; explicit selection still works.
quiz.explanation: It controls implicit selection, not the permissions or correctness of an explicitly invoked workflow.

quiz.question: A child says it used readme-check. What is the best next check?
options: Assume every inherited skill ran automatically.
Inspect the actual instruction source and compare findings with the supplied README.
Increase the number of subagents until the reports agree.
quiz.explanation: Inheritance and self-report do not establish correct invocation or a grounded result; inspect the evidence.

quiz.question: Two installed skills have the same name. What should you do?
options: Inspect their paths and actual selection; Codex does not merge their instructions.
Assume the project's version always wins under Claude's precedence rules.
Combine their files automatically without reviewing conflicts.
quiz.explanation: Duplicate packages can both appear. Identify the source actually used before changing or evaluating it.

quiz.question: What does a healthy MCP connection prove?
options: Every returned statement is current and accurate.
The connection can initialize; correct retrieval and task authorization still need checking.
All tools on the underlying service are authorized for this task.
quiz.explanation: Connection health is one layer. The operation, record, source and delegated action still require verification.

quiz.question: The server appears in a list, but the first call returns an authentication error. What is established?
options: Registration worked; authorization and retrieval have not yet succeeded.
The installation is complete and all tools are ready.
Increasing model reasoning will supply the missing credential.
quiz.explanation: Different layers can succeed independently. Inspect authentication rather than declaring the whole connection healthy.

quiz.question: A teammate has your project MCP entry but cannot read a private ticket. What is a likely distinction?
options: The project file must contain your token value.
All MCP configuration must be global to retrieve records.
Configuration sharing does not supply the teammate's service authorization.
quiz.explanation: A connection definition and an authenticated identity are separate; each user needs appropriate service access.

quiz.question: A Markdown export of a remote record was attached yesterday. What can you safely claim?
options: The remote record remains identical because the file was mentioned.
The attached snapshot contains the observed content; current remote state needs checking.
A resource URI automatically keeps the snapshot synchronized.
quiz.explanation: File context provides a particular copy. Its freshness and relationship to the live source must be established separately.

quiz.question: An API guide shows defer_loading and tool_search. What follows for Codex config.toml?
options: Those API fields can be copied directly into any Codex configuration.
Every connected MCP server must expose a tool literally named tool_search.
Nothing automatically; verify the Codex host's documented controls separately.
quiz.explanation: API request schemas and end-user Codex configuration are different surfaces, even when they implement related ideas.

quiz.question: What is the current relationship between app-server and an MCP client?
options: App-server uses a distinct protocol and is not a drop-in MCP server.
An MCP client can launch it under the old command name without changes.
Removing codex mcp-server also removed external MCP connections.
quiz.explanation: The removed hosting interface and external MCP consumption are separate. App-server integration requires protocol changes and a support review.

quiz.question: Which division fits the capstone once the interface is frozen?
options: Both workers rewrite both starter files without an owner.
One worker invents the contract while the other changes tests to match.
A owns normalization, B owns aggregation, and the parent checks their combined result.
quiz.explanation: A and B can work independently against the frozen interface with disjoint file ownership; integration waits for both outputs.

quiz.question: What happens if a custom Codex role claims its own mcp_servers configuration?
options: It automatically creates an isolated connector account.
It does not override the inherited parent MCP configuration.
It grants the role all tools from every server.
quiz.explanation: Configure connections in the parent session. Role prose and unsupported fields do not establish new server access.

quiz.question: Which statement about Codex explorer is accurate for this lesson?
options: It is a documented read-heavy role; task scope and inherited controls still matter.
It is Claude Explore with an identical guaranteed tool list.
It automatically creates a separate Git worktree for every task.
quiz.explanation: Use the documented Codex role and verify actual controls instead of importing behavior from another product.

quiz.question: When should final verification run?
options: At the same time as the worker, against whatever files happen to exist.
After the intended changes are integrated into the files being verified.
Only when every agent reports confidence.
quiz.explanation: Verification must observe the actual final state. Earlier checks cannot establish the correctness of later changes.

quiz.question: A subagent is running in the background. What can the parent safely do?
options: Perform an independent task and wait for the result before making dependent claims.
Mark its requested output complete immediately.
Assume it is now scheduled to rerun automatically.
quiz.explanation: Background execution allows independent progress. It establishes neither completion nor recurrence.

quiz.question: A worker reports tests passed in its worktree. What remains before delivery?
options: Verify every external service is a copy of production.
Delete the worktree immediately because all work is already in Local.
Review and integrate the intended changes, then check the destination state.
quiz.explanation: A worktree result is evidence about that checkout. Integration can change the final state and needs its own verification.

quiz.question: What does a depends-on column in a Markdown task ledger do?
options: Automatically blocks every child until its dependency succeeds.
Records a dependency that the coordinator must enforce.
Creates Claude's shared task-list feature inside Codex.
quiz.explanation: The ledger makes the dependency visible. Actual orchestration still requires the parent to route and wait for the right work.

quiz.question: What makes a hook operationally meaningful?
options: A script with a memorable filename.
Any instruction that says always.
A supported event, a runnable handler, and a tested result contract.
quiz.explanation: A hook is an event-to-handler integration. Naming a script or repeating an instruction does not establish when it runs or how Codex interprets its result.

quiz.question: What happens if one active layer contains hooks.json and inline hooks?
options: The project becomes automatically trusted.
Codex loads both and warns, so duplicate execution is possible.
The TOML always erases the JSON hooks.
quiz.explanation: The documented behavior is additive. A source inventory and one representation per layer help prevent unintended duplicate handlers.

quiz.question: Can an async command hook stop the action that triggered it?
options: No; background hook output is informational and arrives later.
Yes, if the statusMessage says blocking.
Yes, because JSON always overrides the sandbox.
quiz.explanation: Preventive decisions require a supported synchronous control path. Background output cannot retroactively prevent the triggering operation.

quiz.question: A PostToolUse hook reports that a completed command changed a file. What can it guarantee?
options: It can automatically rewind every changed file.
It proves the command exited successfully.
It can provide documented feedback, but cannot undo the side effect.
quiz.explanation: The event is after execution, and Bash PostToolUse can include unsuccessful commands. Recovery requires a separate, authorized action.

quiz.question: Why is valid JSON not enough to validate a hook?
options: Codex accepts every parsed compatibility field.
Its fields and decisions must also be supported for that event.
JSON automatically executes shell commands.
quiz.explanation: The event-specific contract determines operational behavior. Unsupported fields may cause a failure even when parsing succeeds.

quiz.question: What is the correct description of this lesson's explicit review?
options: A practical alternative to unsupported prompt-hook execution.
Proof that type prompt runs automatically in Codex.
A replacement for all sandbox and approval controls.
quiz.explanation: The source goal is preserved, but the alternative's capabilities and limits must remain explicit.

quiz.question: A handler exits because its runtime path is wrong. What should you conclude?
options: The policy check passed because no warning was printed.
The runtime should be fixed by disabling the sandbox.
The handler failed to launch; blocking behavior still needs separate verification.
quiz.explanation: Launch failure and policy success are different outcomes. Fix the path and verify the event's documented failure behavior.

quiz.question: What should determine whether a task needs advanced features?
options: The number of features available in the menu.
The assumption that more effort always produces a better result.
A concrete uncertainty or execution requirement.
quiz.explanation: Select controls because they solve the task's actual problem. A simple change can be delivered reliably without a complicated workflow.

quiz.question: What is a good reason to ask a planning question?
options: The agent has not yet chosen a variable name.
The answer materially changes scope, behavior, or authorization.
A checklist says every task needs three questions.
quiz.explanation: Questions should resolve consequential uncertainty. Routine implementation choices can usually be handled within the authorized scope.

quiz.question: What is the strongest evidence that a higher effort setting helped?
options: It improves task acceptance on comparable inputs with an acceptable tradeoff.
The answer contains more paragraphs.
The model displays a more impressive setting label.
quiz.explanation: Assess the work produced and its cost in time or usage. UI labels and response length do not establish quality.

quiz.question: Does Approve for me expand writable roots?
options: Yes; it removes all filesystem restrictions.
Only when a hook prints allow.
No; it changes the review path for eligible requests.
quiz.explanation: Automatic review does not itself expand the sandbox or enable networking. It evaluates requests at the existing boundary.

quiz.question: What should happen when a previously expected schedule is missing?
options: Start a hidden loop so monitoring continues.
Reconcile its state and obtain approval before any replacement creation.
Create another one immediately with the same name.
quiz.explanation: Absence is not authorization. A replacement can duplicate effects or revive intentionally stopped work.

quiz.question: What does approval_policy never tell you?
options: Codex does not stop for approval prompts; it does not by itself define the sandbox.
The filesystem is necessarily read-only.
The user authorized all external writes.
quiz.explanation: Approval behavior and sandbox access are independent controls. Neither replaces task-specific authorization.

quiz.question: What does codex exec --json output?
options: Only a single final object with no progress.
A Git commit containing all changes.
A newline-delimited stream of events, not one final JSON object.
quiz.explanation: Consumers must parse JSON Lines appropriately and still inspect failures and the final task result.

quiz.question: An installed plugin cannot read a private record. What follows?
options: Assume the record does not exist.
Install another copy to bypass permissions.
Check its connection, identity, permissions, and record access.
quiz.explanation: Installation is only one setup state. Data access depends on the connected service and the account's actual permissions.

quiz.question: Where should access to an external record ultimately be enforced?
options: In the plugin's icon and display name.
At the connected service/tool boundary, alongside the user's authorized scope.
Only in a friendly description in SKILL.md.
quiz.explanation: Instructions help guide use, but actual external access depends on the service and the identity and permissions used by the connection.

quiz.question: Does a new portable skills-only manifest need a skills field?
options: No; portable skills are discovered from the root skills/ directory.
Yes; otherwise a server must be installed.
Only if its filename starts with a dot.
quiz.explanation: The current portable format uses fixed package locations. Compatibility manifests can use different declarations, so identify the format first.

quiz.question: From where does a local source.path resolve?
options: Always the .agents/plugins folder.
The user's current browser download directory.
The marketplace root.
quiz.explanation: The documented root determines path resolution. Confusing it with the catalog folder can make an entry point to the wrong or missing package.

quiz.question: Offline package validation passed. What may you claim?
options: The public directory approved the plugin.
The checked package structure is valid; client execution remains unverified.
Every user workflow has passed.
quiz.explanation: Verification claims must match the layer actually exercised. Package structure, runtime behavior, and publication review are separate.

quiz.question: A public plugin draft has been approved. Is it necessarily published?
options: No; the publisher chooses when to publish the approved version.
Yes; approval always publishes immediately.
Only if its local manifest contains MIT.
quiz.explanation: The documented flow separates review approval from the explicit publication step. A license field does not change that state.
